source_text: Deus igitur machinator constitutorque rerum, sicut in se- s cundo libro diximus, antequam praeclarum hoc opus mundi adoriretur, sanctum et incorruptibilem spiritum genuit, quem filium nuncuparet. et quamuis alios postea innumerabiles creauisset, quos angelos dicimus, hunc tamen solum primogenitum diuini nominis appellatione dignatus est, patria scilicet uirtute ac maiestate pollentem. esse autem summi dei filium, qui sit potestate maxima praeditus, non tantum congruentes in unum uoces prophetarum, sed etiam Trismegisti praedicatio et Sibyllarum uaticinia demonstrant. Hermes in eo libro qui λόγος τέλειος inscribitur, his usus est uerbis: ὁ κύριος καὶ τῶν πάντων ποιητὴς, ὃν Θεὸν καλεῖν νενομίκαμεν, ἐπεὶ τὸν δεύτερον ἐποίησε θεὸν ὁρατὸν καὶ αἰσθητὸν — αἰσθητὸν δέ φημι οὐ διὰ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι αὐτὸν, περὶ γὰρ τούτου, πότερον αὐτὸς αἰσθάνεται ἣ μή, εἰσαῦθις ῥηθήσεται, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι εἰς αἴσθησιν ὑποπέμπει καὶ εἰς ὅρασιν — ἐπεὶ οὖν τοῦτον ἐποίησε πρῶτον καὶ μόνον καὶ ἕνα, καλὸς δέ αὐτῷ ἐφάνη, καὶ πληρέστατος πάντων τῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἠγάσθη τε καὶ πάνυ ἐφίλησεν ὤς ἴδιον τόκον. Sibylla Erythraea in carminis sui Et rursus in fine eiusdem carminis: principio, quod a summo deo exorsa est, filium dei ducem et imperatorem omnium his uersibus praedicat: παντοτρόφον κτίστην, ὅστις γλυκὺ πνεῦμα ἅπασιν κάτθετο, χἠγητῆρα Θεὸν πάντων ἐποίησεν. et rursus in fine: ἄλλον ἔδωκε Θεὸς πιστοῖς ἀνδράσσι γεραίρειν. et alia Sibylla praecipit hunc oportere cognosci: αὐτὸν σου γίνωσκε Θεὸν Θεοῦ υἱὸν ἐόντα. uidelicet et ipse est dei filius, qui per Solomonem sapientissimum regem diuino spiritu plenum locutus est ea quae subiecimus: dominus condidit me initium uiarum suarum in opera sua, ante saeculum fundauit me: in principio antequam terram faceret et antequam abyssos constitueret, priusquam procederent fontes aquarum, ante omnes colles genuit me. dominus fecit regiones et fines inhabitabiles sub caelo. cum pararet caelum, aderam illi, etcum secerneret suam sedem: cum super uentos faceret ualidas nubes et cum confirmatos ponebat fontes sub caelo, quando fortia faciebat fundamenta terrae, eram penes illum disponens. ego eram cui adgaudebat. cottidie autem iucundabar ante faciem eius, cum laetaretur orbe perfecto. idcirco illum Trismegistus δημιουργὸν TOO seou et Sibylla σύμβουλον appellat, quod tanta sapientia et uirtute sit instructus a deo patre, ut consilio eius et manibus uteretur in fabricatione mundi.
pass_a_gloss: God therefore, the contriver and establisher of things, as we said in the second book, before this glorious work of the world was begun, generated a holy and incorruptible Spirit, whom He would call Son. And although He created many others afterwards, whom we call angels, He nevertheless deemed this one alone, the firstborn, worthy of the divine name, clearly because He was powerful with paternal virtue and majesty. That He is the Son of the highest God, who is endowed with the greatest power, is demonstrated not only by the congruent voices of the prophets, but also by the prediction of Trismegistus and the prophecies of the Sibyls. Hermes, in that book which is inscribed 'The Perfect Word', used these words: 'The Lord and maker of all things, whom we are accustomed to call God, since He made a second God, visible and perceptible — I say perceptible, not because He perceives, for it will be said again whether He perceives or not, but because He sends into perception and into sight — since therefore He made this one first and alone and single, He seemed good to Him, and most full of all good things, He delighted in Him and loved Him exceedingly as His own offspring.' And the Erythraean Sibyl, in the beginning of her poem, and again at the end of the same poem, predicts the Son of God, the leader and commander of all, in these verses: 'The all-nourishing creator, who placed a sweet spirit in all, made God the leader of all.' And again at the end: 'God gave another to faithful men to reverence.' And another Sibyl commands that this one ought to be recognized: 'Know Him as the Son of God, being God.' Clearly, He is also the Son of God, who spoke through Solomon, the wisest king, full of the divine Spirit, the things which we have subjoined: 'The Lord founded me, the beginning of His ways, in His works; He established me before the century; in the beginning, before He made the earth, and before He established the abysses, before the springs of waters proceeded, He generated me before all the hills. The Lord made the regions and the boundaries of the inhabitable places under the heaven. When He was preparing the heaven, I was with Him; when He was separating His seat, when He was making strong clouds over the winds, and when He was setting the established springs under the heaven, when He was making the strong foundations of the earth, I was with Him, arranging. I was the one in whom He delighted. But I was daily rejoicing before His face, when He was rejoicing in the perfect orb. Therefore, Trismegistus calls Him the 'demiurge' and the Sibyl calls Him 'counselor', because He is instructed with such great wisdom and virtue by God the Father, that He uses His counsel and hands in the fabrication of the world.

pass_b_english: God is the contriver and establisher of all things, as we stated in the second book. Before He undertook this glorious work of the world, He generated a holy and incorruptible Spirit, whom He would call Son. Although He later created countless others, whom we call angels, He deemed this one alone, the firstborn, worthy of the divine name, because He was endowed with paternal virtue and majesty. That He is the Son of the Most High God, endowed with the greatest power, is demonstrated not only by the harmonious voices of the prophets, but also by the prediction of Trismegistus and the prophecies of the Sibyls. In the book entitled The Perfect Word, Hermes uses these words: "The Lord and maker of all things, whom we are accustomed to call God, since He made a second God, visible and perceptible — I say perceptible not because He perceives, for it will be said again whether He perceives or not, but because He sends into perception and into sight — since therefore He made this one first and alone and single, He seemed good to Him, and most full of all good things; He delighted in Him and loved Him exceedingly as His own offspring." The Erythraean Sibyl, at the beginning of her poem and again at its end, proclaims the Son of God as the leader and commander of all in these verses: "The all-nourishing creator, who placed a sweet spirit in all, made God the leader of all." And again at the end: "God gave another to faithful men to reverence." Another Sibyl commands that this one must be recognized: "Know Him as the Son of God, being God." Clearly, He is also the Son of God who spoke through Solomon, the wisest king, full of the divine Spirit, the words we have subjoined: "The Lord founded me as the beginning of His ways, for His works; He established me before the age; in the beginning, before He made the earth, and before He established the abysses, before the springs of waters proceeded, He generated me before all the hills. The Lord made the regions and the boundaries of the habitable places under heaven. When He was preparing heaven, I was with Him; when He was setting His throne in place, when He was making strong clouds over the winds, and when He was fixing the established springs under heaven, when He was laying the strong foundations of the earth, I was beside Him, arranging. I was the one in whom He delighted. Daily I rejoiced before His face, when He rejoiced in the completed world" (Proverbs 8:22-31). Therefore Trismegistus calls Him the demiurge and the Sibyl calls Him counselor, because He is so instructed with wisdom and virtue by God the Father that He employs His counsel and hands in the fabrication of the world.
